subtopic: Triton / Differential correctness testing under FP non-associativity
learningObjective: Reason about tolerance selection when a Triton kernel's reduction order differs from a reference implementation.
stem: You wrote a Triton FP16-in/FP32-accumulate matmul kernel and compare its FP32 output against `torch.matmul(a.float(), b.float())` (also FP32). You observe max absolute error ~5e-3 and max relative error ~1e-3 on random inputs with K=4096. Which conclusion is best supported?
codeSnippet:
# a: [M, K] FP16 row-major; b: [K, N] FP16 row-major; K = 4096
# y = my_kernel(a, b)          # Triton kernel: FP16 in, FP32 accum, FP32 out
# y_ref = torch.matmul(a.float(), b.float())   # FP32 reference
#
# Observed:
# torch.max(torch.abs(y - y_ref)).item()                              # ~5e-3
# torch.max(torch.abs(y - y_ref) / (torch.abs(y_ref) + 1e-6)).item()  # ~1e-3

options.text: The reference `torch.matmul(a.float(), b.float())` is itself imprecise on GPU because PyTorch uses TF32 by default on Ampere; the observed error is entirely from the reference and the Triton kernel is exact.

The discrepancy indicates a bug in the kernel: FP32 accumulators guarantee bit-identical output to an FP32 reference, so any deviation above the FP32 machine epsilon (~1e-7) implies an incorrect implementation.

The discrepancy is consistent with expected FP16-input matmul precision: FP16 has ~11 mantissa bits (~3 decimal digits), so per-element rounding accumulates over K=4096 reductions. The observed rtol ~1e-3 is a reasonable tolerance for FP16-input GEMM against an FP32-input reference; the kernel is likely correct.

The discrepancy is due to CUDA's non-determinism; the same kernel will produce a different result each run, so absolute tolerance measurement is meaningless and the test should use `torch.testing.assert_close(atol=inf, rtol=inf)` to always pass.

explanation: The kernel takes FP16 inputs and accumulates in FP32; the reference upcasts inputs to FP32 first (no FP16 rounding). The primary error source is FP16 input rounding — each of 4096 accumulated products contributes a small error, and errors partially cancel but do not vanish. Empirically, FP16-input matmul is expected to differ from FP32-input matmul by roughly rtol ~1e-3 at moderate K, which matches the observation. Choice B is wrong: FP32 accumulation reduces but does not eliminate FP16-input rounding. C fabricates non-determinism and rejects tolerance testing. D partially points at a real issue (TF32 on Ampere for `float()` inputs would introduce error), but the observed error is dominated by FP16 rounding.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: while TF32 default on Ampere can complicate references, the FP16-input error dominates here.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: FP32 accum does not restore FP16-input precision.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: rtol ~1e-3 is consistent with FP16-input matmul error at K=4096.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: modern GPU matmul is largely deterministic per algorithm; tolerance is the right tool.

assumptions: FP16 has ~11 mantissa bits (relative machine epsilon ~9.77e-4).
Random inputs with reasonable range; no NaN/inf pathologies.
nonImplications: Does not imply the kernel is guaranteed correct — a proper test should include edge cases (extreme values, dimension boundaries).
Does not imply this tolerance applies to all dtypes; FP8 or INT8 kernels have very different acceptable error bands.

distractorRationales.A: Wrong attribution of the error source.
distractorRationales.B: Confuses accumulator precision with input precision.
